tldr: A causal difference of Gini coefficients can cancel the linear effect of an infinite-variance common tail mean. The research question is the cost of confidence intervals that must cover the full common-tail experiment even at laws near that cancellation. The focal object is an explicit expected-length frontier over every slope neighborhood, attained by one observable interval without receiving the neighborhood radius. A six-moment projection construction and normalized shared-tail tests provide the two sides of the problem. The nonlinear lower separation must remain legal uniformly in the radius, and the upper width must be controlled on every sample outcome. The resulting boundary distinguishes a square-integrable first-order calculation from honest uncertainty about inequality effects.
gap: Existing causal inequality derivatives, single-Gini tail limits, and Gaussian interval-adaptation theory do not provide the inspected theorem-level answer for common-tail Gini cancellation with ambient coverage and localized expected length.
fill: The core asks for an explicit frontier, a radius-free total interval, and all-randomized-interval lower bounds in that exact experiment. Public-curvature-preserving alternatives and unconditional projection width make the uniformity requirement concrete.
